group.passage: Floating on its back and cracking open a clam on its chest, the sea otter looks more like a playful pet than a guardian of forests. Yet along the rocky coasts of the North Pacific, this small animal helps keep whole forests beneath the waves alive. The animal's secret lies in its huge appetite. It has no thick layer of fat, as seals and whales do, to protect it from the cold. Instead, it depends on its fur, which is so dense that a single square inch can hold up to a million hairs, about ten times as many as on an entire human head. Staying warm this way burns a great deal of energy, so an adult must eat 20 to 30 percent of its body weight every day. Its menu includes clams, crabs, snails and sea urchins, and it often uses a rock as a tool to break open hard shells. Those sea urchins are the key to the story. Urchins feed on kelp, a giant seaweed that can grow up to two feet a day and forms forests full of fish and other sea life. Where otters live in healthy numbers, they keep these spiny animals under control. Where otters disappear, the urchins multiply rapidly and can strip the forests bare. This is why scientists describe the sea otter as a keystone species, one whose presence holds an entire ecosystem together. Because of their valuable fur, sea otters were hunted almost to extinction between 1741 and 1911. Before the hunting began, there may have been as many as 300,000 of them; by the early 1900s, only about 13 small groups survived. A treaty signed in 1911 finally protected them, and in the late 1960s, 413 otters were moved to Southeast Alaska, where their numbers recovered. Today, about 3,000 southern sea otters live along the coast of California, but they have returned to only about 13 percent of their former range. Farther north, in waters the otters have not yet returned to, the kelp canopy along the 217 miles of coast between San Francisco and the Oregon border has shrunk by more than 90 percent after a marine heat wave and a population boom of purple sea urchins.

translation_zh.text:
海獺守護海藻林

海獺仰躺著漂浮在水面上，在胸口敲開蛤蜊，看起來比較像一隻愛玩的寵物，而不是森林的守護者。然而在北太平洋多岩石的海岸邊，這種小動物幫忙讓整片海面下的森林得以存活。

這種動物的祕密就在牠驚人的食量。牠不像海豹和鯨魚那樣有一層厚厚的脂肪來抵擋寒冷，而是靠毛皮保暖；牠的毛非常濃密，一平方英寸就可能有多達一百萬根毛，大約是一整顆人頭頭髮數量的十倍。用這種方式保暖要消耗大量的能量，所以一隻成年海獺每天必須吃下體重 20% 到 30% 的食物。牠的菜單包括蛤蜊、螃蟹、螺類和海膽，而且牠常常拿石頭當工具，敲開堅硬的外殼。

這些海膽正是故事的關鍵。海膽以海藻為食；海藻是一種巨大的藻類，一天最多可以長兩英尺，並形成充滿魚類和其他海洋生物的森林。在海獺數量健康的地方，牠們能控制這些長滿刺的動物。在海獺消失的地方，海膽快速繁殖，可能把整片森林啃得精光。這就是為什麼科學家把海獺稱為「關鍵物種」——牠的存在把整個生態系撐在一起。

因為毛皮珍貴，海獺在 1741 年到 1911 年間被獵捕到幾乎滅絕。獵捕開始之前，海獺可能多達 30 萬隻；到了 1900 年代初，只剩下大約 13 個小族群倖存。1911 年簽訂的一項條約終於保護了牠們；1960 年代末，又有 413 隻海獺被遷移到阿拉斯加東南部，牠們的數量在那裡恢復了。

如今，大約有 3,000 隻南方海獺生活在加州沿岸，但牠們只回到原本分布範圍的大約 13%。再往北，在海獺還沒有回去的海域，從舊金山到奧勒岡州界 217 英里長的海岸，在一場海洋熱浪與紫海膽數量暴增之後，海藻冠層已經縮小了九成以上。
